name: Low Lunar Orbit
story: The closest band to the lunar surface — typically 50 to 100 km up. Spacecraft here can image the surface at sub-metre resolution but pay a steep price: the Moon's mass distribution is wildly uneven (giant subsurface mascons under the maria), so a low orbit perturbs aggressively. Most LLO missions need active station-keeping or a carefully chosen 'frozen' inclination that resists the drift. LRO has flown here continuously since 2009 — the longest-lived lunar mission.
comparison: About 1/3,800th of the way back to Earth. From LLO the Moon's horizon is sharply curved — you can see 30-40 km in any direction before the surface drops off.
